title: The Bauhaus: Weimar, Dessau, Berlin, 1919–1933
subtitle: The art school in Weimar, Dessau and Berlin, from Gropius's manifesto to self-dissolution
intro: In April 1919, five months after the armistice and in the city where a national assembly was drafting Germany's first democratic constitution, the architect Walter Gropius merged two Weimar art schools and called the result the Bauhaus. His manifesto promised to put painters, sculptors and craftsmen back into one workshop and to build a new world together. In fourteen years the school moved twice, changed directors three times, and outlived three governments that wanted it closed, until its own faculty dissolved it in Berlin in July 1933 rather than accept the conditions of the new regime.

This chapter sets the school's people side by side. Oskar Schlemmer's diary and letters are the frankest running commentary on its quarrels. Lyonel Feininger wrote to his wife whenever they were apart, Paul Klee to Lily, and Ise Gropius kept a near-daily chronicle of the director's office from 1924 to 1928. Weavers and metalworkers such as Gunta Stölzl, Anni Albers and Marianne Brandt show the workshops from the bench, where women often began in the jobs the school assigned them and ended up running departments.

Much of the honest record here is not diary at all. It is manifestos, circulars, published essays, faculty protocols, and the minutes and votes of the bodies that paid for the school: the Thuringian Landtag in Weimar and the city council of Dessau. These are tagged as what they are. Several diaries, Ise Gropius's among them, are recent publications. Everything is paraphrased, apart from two of the school's own world-famous slogans.

The convergences fall on the days when these people were in the same rooms: the founding, the exhibition summer of 1923 with its model house and the Triadic Ballet, the masters' self-dissolution at Christmas 1924, the opening of Gropius's glass building in Dessau in December 1926, the handovers of 1928 and 1930, and the last weeks in a disused telephone factory in Berlin-Steglitz.

Two kinds of conflict run through the record. Inside the school the masters fought over mysticism and industry, art and social use, and over whether a school could keep out of politics; Hannes Meyer's dismissal in 1930 is reported here as each side described it. Outside it, nationalist and later National Socialist parties attacked the Bauhaus from the first year as foreign, Bolshevist and degenerate, and once in power they closed it. That hostility is set out as the councils, police and Gestapo recorded it.

eyes.name: Walter Gropius
eyes.role: Architect, aged 35 at the founding; director of the Bauhaus 1919–1928
eyes.where: Weimar 1919–25, Dessau 1925–28, then a private practice in Berlin
eyes.form: manifesto, circulars to the masters, lectures and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: The April 1919 manifesto and programme survive in many printed copies; his circulars, Masters' Council minutes and correspondence are held mainly at the Bauhaus-Archiv Berlin and the Houghton Library, Harvard, and are excerpted in Hans M. Wingler's documentary history. Digest only.
eyes.bio: A front-line veteran of the First World War, Gropius merged the Weimar art academy and the former school of arts and crafts into one school and named it the Bauhaus. He spent nine years defending it to state governments, councils and the press, and changed its course more than once, most visibly in 1922–23 when he turned it from craft mysticism towards industry.

sources.title: Bauhaus Kooperation: What exactly was the Bauhaus?

eyes.name: Lyonel Feininger
eyes.role: American-born painter and printmaker, aged 47 in 1919; first master appointed, later head of the printing workshop
eyes.where: Weimar 1919–25, Dessau master's house 1926–33; summers on the Baltic at Deep
eyes.authenticity: Feininger wrote to Julia Feininger almost daily whenever they were apart; the letters are held in the Feininger papers at the Houghton Library, Harvard, and are quoted in exhibition catalogues. Only letters seen quoted with their dates are used here.
eyes.bio: Feininger cut the woodcut cathedral that stood on the cover of the 1919 manifesto and stayed with the school, without teaching duties after 1925, until its end. His letters to Julia are the steadiest private running commentary on the school from a master who was never a partisan of any of its factions.

sources.title: Kathedrale: title page for the Bauhaus manifesto (German History in Documents and Images)
Ludorff catalogue: Lyonel Feininger (quoting letters to Julia, 1924 and 1933)

eyes.name: Johannes Itten
eyes.role: Swiss painter and teacher, aged 31 on arrival; master of the preliminary course 1919–23
eyes.where: Vienna until 1919, Weimar 1919–23, then the Mazdaznan community at Herrliberg near Zurich
eyes.vantage_label: the teacher at the centre of the first crisis
eyes.form: diaries and notebooks; later autobiographical writing
eyes.authenticity: Itten kept diaries and teaching notebooks; the earlier volumes were published as Johannes Itten, Die Tagebücher (ed. Eva Badura-Triska, 1990). His accounts of the Weimar years are largely later and autobiographical, and are marked as such.
eyes.bio: Itten came from Vienna, where he had run a private art school, and brought several of his students with him. His preliminary course — breathing exercises, rhythm, contrast studies, old-master analysis — became the Bauhaus's foundation, while his Mazdaznan regime of diet and meditation split the school.

eyes.name: Oskar Schlemmer
eyes.role: Painter, sculptor and stage designer, aged 32 on arrival; master of the mural and sculpture workshops, then of the Bauhaus stage
eyes.authenticity: Published by his widow as Oskar Schlemmer: Briefe und Tagebücher (ed. Tut Schlemmer, Munich 1958); English edition The Letters and Diaries of Oskar Schlemmer (1972). The edition is selected and some passages are trimmed; digest only.
eyes.bio: Schlemmer designed the Bauhaus emblem and ran the experimental stage, and he recorded the school's quarrels more frankly than anyone else. He saw the Bauhaus as a contest of personalities and ideas, and wrote about it with irony and affection, before leaving in 1929.

sources.title: Kirkus review: The Letters and Diaries of Oskar Schlemmer

eyes.name: Paul Klee
eyes.role: Swiss-German painter, aged 41 on appointment; master of the bookbinding, glass-painting and weaving form classes, and lecturer on form
eyes.where: Weimar 1921–25 (commuting from Munich until October 1921), Dessau 1926–31, Düsseldorf 1931–33, Bern from December 1933
eyes.form: dated letters (to his wife Lily and family); teaching notes
eyes.authenticity: Klee's diaries end in 1918; for the Bauhaus years the record is his letters to Lily Klee and the family (Briefe an die Familie, ed. Felix Klee, 1979) and his teaching notes (Beiträge zur bildnerischen Formlehre, 1921–22, digitised by the Zentrum Paul Klee). Felix Klee's documentary biography adds dated family memories.
eyes.bio: Klee taught at the Bauhaus for ten years while insisting that he was first of all a working painter. His letters are full of studio light, teaching duties eating his time, and family news, and they record the school's ceremonies and crises only in passing.

sources.title: Felix Klee, Paul Klee: His Life and Work in Documents (1962), Monoskop

eyes.name: Wassily Kandinsky
eyes.role: Russian painter and theorist, aged 56 on arrival; master of the wall-painting workshop and teacher of analytical drawing
eyes.where: Moscow until December 1921; Weimar 1922–25, Dessau 1925–32, Berlin 1932–33, then Neuilly near Paris
eyes.vantage_label: senior master, to the last meeting
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Schoenberg and others survive and are published (Schoenberg's side in Arnold Schoenberg: Letters, ed. Erwin Stein). His Bauhaus book Punkt und Linie zu Fläche appeared in 1926. No diary for these years is used.
eyes.bio: Kandinsky arrived from revolutionary Moscow and stayed through every phase of the school, from Weimar to the final vote in Berlin. He backed Meyer's removal in 1930 and was one of the masters the new regime named as unacceptable in 1933.

sources.title: Facing History: Antisemitism and Jewish Identity in Weimar Germany (Schoenberg–Kandinsky letters)

eyes.name: Gunta Stölzl
eyes.role: Student from October 1919 (aged 22), journeyman 1923, weaving workshop teacher from 1925 and its head (the only woman master) 1927–31
eyes.where: Weimar 1919–25 (with 1924 in Herrliberg), Dessau 1925–31, Zurich from 1931
eyes.vantage_label: weaver who became the only woman master
eyes.form: diary, dated letters and later reminiscence
eyes.authenticity: Her First World War and 1919 diaries and her letters are held by her estate and the Bauhaus-Archiv and have been excerpted in exhibition catalogues; her account of the workshop's early years was written later. Entries here rely on dated letters and dated facts; diary passages are not quoted.
eyes.bio: Stölzl had nursed with the Red Cross behind the front before coming to Weimar. She turned a workshop that the school had treated as a place to put its women into its most commercially successful department, and she left after a campaign against her in 1931.

sources.title: Gunta Stölzl: textile and weaving workshop 1919–1931 (Bauhaus Bookshelf)

eyes.name: Anni Albers (née Fleischmann)
eyes.role: Student from 1922 (aged 23), weaver; married Josef Albers in 1925
eyes.where: Weimar 1922–25, Dessau 1925–31, Berlin, then Black Mountain College, North Carolina, from November 1933
eyes.authenticity: Her early essays (from 1924) and diploma work are documented by the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation and the Bauhaus-Archiv; most of her account of the Bauhaus was written later in English. Entries here are marked approx where only the year or month is secure.
eyes.bio: Albers came to the Bauhaus wanting to paint and was steered into weaving, which she later said she first took up reluctantly. Her diploma fabric for Meyer's trade-union school shows the Meyer years' turn to light, sound-absorbing, practical cloth.

eyes.name: Marianne Brandt
eyes.role: Painter who entered the Bauhaus in 1924 (aged 30); metal workshop student, then deputy and acting head of the workshop 1928–29
eyes.where: Weimar 1924–25, Dessau 1925–29, then Gropius's Berlin office and industry
eyes.vantage_label: the woman in the metal workshop
eyes.authenticity: Her designs are dated by Bauhaus workshop records and survive in museum collections. Her description of her reception in the workshop comes from a letter to the younger generation written decades later, around 1970, and is marked as later memory.
eyes.bio: Brandt was admitted to a workshop where women were not expected and, by her own later account, was first handed the dullest tasks. Her small metal teapots and her lamps for industry became some of the best-known Bauhaus objects.

eyes.name: Ise Gropius (née Ilse Frank)
eyes.role: Writer and editor, married Walter Gropius in October 1923; the school's unofficial publicist and chronicler
eyes.vantage_label: the director's wife, writing a daily chronicle
eyes.authenticity: Her diary of 1 September 1924 to 13 March 1928, which she called a chronicle or daily reportage, is held at the Bauhaus-Archiv Berlin and was published in 2026 as Ise Gropius: Tagebuch 1924–1928. Eine Bauhaus-Chronik (ed. Astrid Bähr and Adriana Kapsreiter, Hirmer). Only entries described in published reviews are used.
eyes.bio: Ise Gropius handled correspondence, publicity and guests for the school and kept a near-daily record of the crisis years, the move to Dessau and her husband's resignation. She saw the institution from the director's desk and dinner table at once.

sources.title: Der Freitag: review of Ise Gropius, Tagebuch 1924–1928

eyes.name: Hannes Meyer
eyes.role: Swiss architect, aged 37 on arrival; head of the new architecture department from 1927, director 1928–1930
eyes.authenticity: His programme essays (notably 'bauen', 1928) and his open letter after his dismissal (August 1930) were published at the time; his papers are at the Deutsches Architekturmuseum, Frankfurt. The date of the open letter's publication is given as mid-August 1930.
eyes.bio: Meyer wanted the school to design for the needs of ordinary people rather than for taste, and pushed it towards collective architecture, standardisation and social research. To his supporters he made the Bauhaus useful; to the city and some masters he let it become a political battleground.

eyes.name: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
eyes.authenticity: Mies kept no diary for these years. The record is official: the lease of the Steglitz factory, the 20 July 1933 protocol of the faculty meeting, and his 10 August 1933 letter to students, held at the Bauhaus-Archiv and the Museum of Modern Art's Mies archive. His later accounts of negotiating with Nazi officials are recollections and are not used for dates.
eyes.bio: Mies was brought in to depoliticise the school and turned it into a stricter school of architecture. He then moved it privately to Berlin when Dessau closed it, and ended it himself rather than accept the regime's conditions.

sources.title: smow: July 19th 1933 – Bauhaus closes. For ever.

eyes.name: Thuringian Landtag and Dessau city council (records and press)
eyes.role: The public bodies that funded, attacked and finally closed the school, and the newspapers that reported them
eyes.side: State of Thuringia; city of Dessau
eyes.where: Weimar (Thuringian Landtag) and Dessau town hall
eyes.authenticity: Landtag debates, budget decisions, council votes and newspaper reports survive in the Thuringian State Archive (Weimar), the Dessau city archive and the Bauhaus-Archiv's chronologies. Vote figures are those given in the institutional chronologies.
eyes.bio: These records are not a single person's eye but the school's audience with the power of the purse. They show the nationalist and later National Socialist hostility as the councils and parties expressed it, from interpellations in Weimar to the closing vote in Dessau.

sources.title: 1932: Dessau closure (Pure Bauhaus, citing Bauhaus-Archiv and Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau chronologies)

entries.headline: The manifesto: all arts back to the workshop
entries.digest: Gropius published a four-page leaflet setting out the programme of the new school. It called on artists to abandon academic separation and train as craftsmen, with the building of the future as the common work, and promised masters, journeymen and apprentices instead of professors and students.
entries.quote: Architects, sculptors, painters, we must all return to the crafts!
entries.source_note: Manifesto and programme of the Staatliches Bauhaus, April 1919 (GHDI facsimile page).

entries.headline: A woodcut cathedral for the cover
entries.digest: Feininger's woodcut on the manifesto's title page showed a Gothic church shattered into crystalline facets, with three stars of light over its spires. The image tied the school to medieval guild building rather than to machines, a reading the school would later have to live down.
entries.source_note: GHDI: 'Kathedrale', title page by Lyonel Feininger for the Bauhaus manifesto; Bauhaus Kooperation object page 'Cathedral'.

entries.headline: The name 'Staatliches Bauhaus in Weimar' is approved
entries.digest: The provisional government in Weimar approved the new name for the merged schools, the date the Bauhaus itself treats as its founding. Funding, buildings and staff all still belonged to the old institutions.
entries.source_note: Standard founding date in Bauhaus-Archiv and Bauhaus Kooperation chronologies.

entries.headline: Itten arrives from Vienna with his students
entries.digest: Itten arrived in Weimar, bringing a group of students from his private school in Vienna. His preliminary course began with physical exercises and breathing, then moved to studies of materials, textures and contrasts, and to the analysis of old-master paintings by rhythm and line.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation, 'A Mystic Milieu' (Itten arrives October 1919); course content from later accounts by Itten and his students.

entries.headline: The first Bauhaus Christmas
entries.digest: In a letter at the end of 1919 Stölzl described the school's Christmas celebration as overwhelmingly beautiful and unlike anything she had known. Festivals and parties became one of the ways the poor and hungry young school held itself together.
entries.source_note: Letter of end 1919, cited in the Bauhaus Bookshelf page on Stölzl and the weaving workshop.

entries.headline: Itten publishes the folio 'Utopia'
entries.digest: Itten and the writer Bruno Adler issued Utopia: Dokumente der Wirklichkeit, a portfolio mixing hand-lettered texts, mystical greetings and reproductions of art across the ages. It showed the Bauhaus at its most visionary and least practical.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation, 'A Mystic Milieu' (folio caption dated 1921).

entries.headline: News of his mother's death reaches Klee in Weimar
entries.digest: Klee was in Weimar, newly teaching, when his mother Ida died in Bern. His son later recorded that Klee had been in his studio that afternoon when the telegram came.
entries.source_note: Felix Klee, Paul Klee: His Life and Work in Documents (1962).

entries.headline: Kandinsky arrives from Moscow
entries.digest: Kandinsky, who had left Soviet Russia at the end of 1921, joined the Bauhaus as master of the wall-painting workshop. He brought a systematic theory of colour and form that sat alongside Klee's more poetic teaching.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation and Bauhaus-Archiv biographies (appointment 1922). Felix Klee's 1962 book gives 1921 in error.

entries.headline: Journeyman's examination as the workshops furnish the model house
entries.digest: Stölzl passed her journeyman's examination in 1923, the year the weaving workshop supplied carpets and fabrics for the exhibition house. The workshop was already selling its rugs and cloth, earning money the school badly needed.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation biography (journeyman's exam 1923); Bauhaus Bookshelf page on the weaving workshop.

entries.headline: Itten leaves; Moholy-Nagy takes the preliminary course
entries.digest: Itten left Weimar for the Mazdaznan community at Herrliberg on Lake Zurich. His successor, the Hungarian constructivist László Moholy-Nagy, turned the course towards materials, technique and machines.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (March 1923).

entries.headline: An interpellation against the Bauhaus in the Landtag
entries.digest: Right-wing deputies raised a formal interpellation against the school in the Thuringian parliament. Since 1919 local craftsmen, nationalist artists and conservative papers had attacked it as foreign, Bolshevist and wasteful, and the government in Weimar pressed it to show results.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (16 March 1923).

entries.headline: An exchange with Schoenberg over rumoured antisemitism
entries.digest: Kandinsky had sounded out his old friend Arnold Schoenberg about directing the music school in Weimar. Schoenberg, told by a third party that antisemitism was rife at the Bauhaus and that Kandinsky shared it, refused in angry letters, and Kandinsky replied with pained denials.
entries.source_note: Arnold Schoenberg: Letters, ed. Erwin Stein (letters of April and May 1923), as quoted by Facing History; days not confirmed here.

entries.headline: The Bauhaus as a contest of spirits
entries.digest: Schlemmer noted in his diary that a struggle of minds was being fought at the Bauhaus, both in the open and in secret, as perhaps nowhere else. The entry came weeks before the exhibition that Gropius hoped would prove the school's worth to its paymasters.
entries.source_note: Diary, June 1923: Oskar Schlemmer, Briefe und Tagebücher (Munich 1958), p. 147, cited by Ulrike Bestgen, Klassik Stiftung Weimar Jahrbuch 2009.

entries.headline: Triadic Ballet and the workshop murals on show
entries.digest: During Bauhaus Week Schlemmer's Triadic Ballet was performed, and visitors saw his murals and reliefs in the stairwell of the workshop building. His manifesto for the exhibition, with its talk of a cathedral of socialism, was withdrawn before distribution because of its political charge, though some copies had already gone out.
entries.source_note: schlemmer.org (August 1923 Bauhaus Week); LeMO (1923 murals); modernism-in-architecture.org on the 1923 manifesto. Exact day of the ballet not confirmed.

entries.headline: Exhibition opens: 'Art and technology, a new unity'
entries.digest: The first Bauhaus exhibition opened with a week of lectures, concerts and stage works. Gropius lectured under his new slogan uniting art and technology, and the model house am Horn, designed by Georg Muche and fitted out by the workshops, was open to visitors until 30 September.
entries.quote: Art and technology – a new unity
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (Bauhaus Week 15–19 August; exhibition to 30 September 1923).

entries.headline: A painter enters the metal workshop
entries.digest: Brandt, already a trained painter, joined the metal workshop under Moholy-Nagy. Writing decades later, she remembered being given the dullest jobs at first, as the men in the workshop doubted a woman belonged there; within months she was designing small teapots and infusers in brass and silver.
entries.source_note: Workshop records of 1924 designs; Brandt's later 'letter to the younger generation' (memoir, c. 1970).

entries.headline: Elections bring a right-wing government to Thuringia
entries.digest: State elections replaced the Social Democratic government that had protected the Bauhaus with a conservative-nationalist coalition dependent on the far right. The new majority had campaigned against the school.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (February 1924).

entries.headline: Colours on the Baltic that cannot be described
entries.digest: On his first summer at the fishing village of Deep, Feininger wrote to Julia that the colours he saw by the sea were beyond description. While Weimar's politicians were debating the school's future, he was gathering the coastal motifs he painted for the next decade.
entries.source_note: Letter to Julia Feininger, 7 July 1924, quoted in Ludorff gallery catalogue, Lyonel Feininger.

entries.headline: Ise Gropius begins her daily chronicle
entries.digest: Ise Gropius opened her diary with one of her husband's maxims: failure comes from failing to persuade, and leadership carries a duty to succeed. She began it as the crisis came to a head, and kept it as a running report on the school.
entries.source_note: Ise Gropius, Tagebuch 1924–1928 (Hirmer 2026), first entry, as described in the Freitag review.

entries.headline: Anni Albers writes on Bauhaus weaving
entries.digest: Albers, a student in the weaving workshop, published a short essay on its work in the youth magazine Junge Menschen, which devoted an issue to the Bauhaus. She described weaving as a field where new structures could be invented on the loom itself.
entries.source_note: Anni Albers, 'Bauhausweberei', Junge Menschen 5, no. 8 (November 1924); month as cited in Albers bibliographies, not checked against the issue.

entries.headline: The masters dissolve the Weimar Bauhaus
entries.digest: After the state had given every master precautionary notice in September and cut the budget to about a third in November, Gropius and the masters published a declaration that they would leave when their contracts ran out, dissolving the school before the state could. Several cities, among them Frankfurt and Mannheim, were sounded out as new homes.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (September, November and 26 December 1924); Ise Gropius's diary records the search for a site (Freitag review).

entries.headline: Dessau votes to take over the Bauhaus
entries.digest: Dessau's city council, led by mayor Fritz Hesse, voted to take over the school against objections from the right. The industrial town, home of the Junkers aircraft works, offered money for a new building and houses for the masters.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (24 March 1925).

entries.headline: Lower case only
entries.digest: Ise Gropius recorded that the school had officially adopted lower-case lettering for its printed matter, with a remark from Gropius on his own persistence. The rule became one of the Bauhaus's most recognisable habits.
entries.source_note: Ise Gropius, Tagebuch, entry of 18 September 1925 (Freitag review). The Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology gives October 1925 for the adoption.

entries.headline: Point and Line to Plane appears
entries.digest: Kandinsky's treatise on the elements of painting was published as the ninth of the Bauhaus books. It set out the analytical method he taught in his drawing classes.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf (Bauhaus book no. 9, 1926).

entries.headline: The weaving workshop moves into the new building
entries.digest: The looms were moved into the new building ahead of its opening. Stölzl reorganised the workshop around training on the loom, dye work and fabrics that could be produced in quantity.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf page on Stölzl (November 1926).

entries.headline: Klee at the dedication festivities
entries.digest: Felix Klee recalled the building's dedication as a festival for the whole community. Klee, who disliked official occasions, took part as one of the school's senior professors.
entries.source_note: Felix Klee (1962), narrative for December 1926.

entries.headline: The glass building opens
entries.digest: Gropius's new school building, with its glass curtain wall over the workshop wing and a bridge carrying offices over the road, was formally opened before a large crowd of guests and press. The city had contributed a substantial subsidy, and the masters became professors of a recognised college.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (4–5 December 1926); Harvard Art Museums photograph of the main entrance on opening day.

entries.headline: A driving test passed
entries.digest: Ise Gropius noted that she had passed her driving test. Her diary mixes such everyday news, trips to the cinema and visiting guests with the school's battles.
entries.source_note: Ise Gropius, Tagebuch, entry of 22 January 1927 (Freitag review).

entries.headline: Meyer opens the architecture department
entries.digest: Hannes Meyer, a Swiss architect known for cooperative housing, began work as head of the school's first regular architecture department. The Bauhaus had promised building since 1919 but had not taught it formally until now.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (1 April 1927).

entries.headline: Gropius announces his resignation
entries.digest: Gropius told the masters he would step down and proposed Meyer as his successor. Moholy-Nagy, Herbert Bayer and Marcel Breuer soon left too.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (3 February 1928).

entries.headline: The chronicle ends
entries.digest: Ise Gropius's diary ends with the handover. In its last months she had written sharply about the new man, including the way he ran his household.
entries.source_note: Ise Gropius, Tagebuch, final entry 13 March 1928 (Freitag review).

entries.headline: Brandt runs the metal workshop
entries.digest: When Moholy-Nagy left, Brandt became acting head of the metal workshop, negotiating with lighting firms that put Bauhaus lamps into production. She left the school in 1929 to work in Gropius's Berlin office.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation and Bauhaus-Archiv biographies (acting head 1928–29).

entries.headline: Meyer becomes director
entries.digest: Meyer took over the school with the aim of putting the people's needs ahead of luxury. He expanded paid work for outside clients, promoted collective design teams and brought in lecturers in economics and sociology.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation biography (director from 1 April 1928).

entries.headline: Schlemmer leaves for Breslau
entries.digest: Schlemmer accepted a post at the Breslau academy and left the Bauhaus. His stage work had sat uneasily with the new director's emphasis on social usefulness, and his letters from the period record his unease with the school's direction.
entries.source_note: LeMO (appointment at Breslau, summer 1929); Briefe und Tagebücher (1958).

entries.headline: Diploma for a fabric that absorbs sound
entries.digest: Albers received her Bauhaus diploma for a wall fabric for the auditorium of the trade-union school at Bernau, designed by Meyer and Hans Wittwer. The cloth combined cellophane and cotton to reflect light and dampen sound.
entries.source_note: Josef and Anni Albers Foundation and Bauhaus-Archiv records; year only.

entries.headline: His Weimar murals are destroyed
entries.digest: On orders from the Thuringian interior ministry under the National Socialist Wilhelm Frick, Schlemmer's 1923 murals in the old Weimar workshop building were painted over. The destruction came while Schlemmer was teaching in Breslau.
entries.source_note: LeMO biography (1930, on Frick's orders).

entries.headline: Kandinsky sides with the mayor
entries.digest: Kandinsky was among those who backed Meyer's removal, arguing that the school's survival depended on keeping party politics out of it. Meyer's supporters saw his removal as a political purge.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation biography of Meyer (Hesse, Gropius and Kandinsky pleaded for the dismissal).

entries.headline: An open letter: 'My expulsion from the Bauhaus'
entries.digest: About two weeks after his dismissal, Meyer published an open letter to Hesse in a Berlin left-wing weekly. He accused the school of having been a style factory and claimed he had fought the 'Bauhaus style' from within.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Hannes Meyer (letter about two weeks after dismissal); publication usually cited as Das Tage-Buch, 16 August 1930, not confirmed here.

entries.headline: Mies van der Rohe appointed
entries.digest: Mies was appointed director, and the school was closed briefly and reopened with new rules. Political activity was banned, and the curriculum was concentrated on architecture.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (1930; starts winter term).

entries.headline: Meyer is dismissed
entries.digest: Mayor Hesse dismissed Meyer without notice, citing communist activity at the school, after months of pressure from the right-wing parties and press. Gropius and Kandinsky had urged the mayor to act to protect the school; students who supported Meyer protested.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation biography of Meyer; Wikipedia (dismissal 1 August 1930).

entries.headline: Stölzl leaves the Bauhaus
entries.digest: Stölzl resigned and moved to Zurich, where she opened her own hand-weaving business. Accounts of her departure link it to agitation against her inside the school, sharpened by her marriage to the Jewish architect Arieh Sharon, which had cost her German citizenship.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation (spring 1931) and Bauhaus Bookshelf (autumn 1931) disagree on the season; the circumstances follow later Bauhaus-Archiv accounts.

entries.headline: Painting the Bauhaus Stairway
entries.digest: In the year the Dessau council closed the school, Schlemmer painted young people climbing the stairs of the Dessau building towards the light of its glass wall. It became the best-known image of the school's spirit.
entries.source_note: LeMO (1932); Museum of Modern Art, Bauhaus Stairway.

entries.headline: Council votes to close the Bauhaus
entries.digest: On a National Socialist motion the Dessau council voted 20 to 5 to close the school. Teaching in Dessau ended when the closure took effect on 1 October.
entries.source_note: Pure Bauhaus (citing Bauhaus-Archiv and Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau chronologies); smow (22 August 1932). Voting details follow those chronologies.

entries.headline: A private Bauhaus in a telephone factory
entries.digest: Mies leased a disused telephone factory in Birkbuschstraße, Steglitz, and reopened the school as a private institute. Students and faculty had to fund it themselves.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (October 1932).

entries.headline: Far from the world's events
entries.digest: Feininger wrote to Julia that the afternoon sun on the sea was intoxicating and that, for now, there was peace there and a great distance from the world's events. In the same letter he asked her to bring only the Chicago Tribune, so he could follow the outside reaction to the boycott of Jewish businesses.
entries.source_note: Letter to Julia Feininger, 9 April 1933, quoted in Ludorff catalogue.

entries.headline: Police search the Berlin Bauhaus
entries.digest: At the request of the Dessau public prosecutor, police and SA men searched the factory building and detained 32 students for a day or two. The building was then sealed.
entries.source_note: Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology; Pure Bauhaus (citing Bauhaus-Archiv).

entries.headline: The faculty votes to dissolve
entries.digest: At a meeting with Kandinsky, Josef Albers, Ludwig Hilberseimer, Walter Peterhans and Lilly Reich, Mies proposed dissolving the school, and the proposal passed unanimously. The protocol gave the hopeless financial position as the reason.
entries.source_note: Protocol dated 20 July 1933 (meeting 19/20 July), as reported by smow and the Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology.

entries.headline: The Gestapo's conditions arrive too late
entries.digest: A letter from the Secret State Police set the terms for any reopening, including the removal of Kandinsky and Hilberseimer and a revised curriculum. By then the faculty had already voted to dissolve.
entries.source_note: Pure Bauhaus (citing Bauhaus-Archiv chronology and Hans Keßler's letters); not confirmed against the original letter.

entries.headline: Mies informs the students
entries.digest: Mies wrote to the students that the faculty had dissolved the Bauhaus, citing its economic situation. The letter said nothing of the police or politics.
entries.source_note: smow; Bauhaus Bookshelf chronology (10 August 1933).

entries.headline: Klee leaves Germany
entries.digest: Dismissed from the Düsseldorf academy that spring, Klee wrote to his son that the furniture had gone and he would leave the following night. He settled in his native Bern.
entries.source_note: Letter to Felix Klee, 22 December 1933, in Felix Klee (1962).

claims.evidence: Manifesto leaflet; GHDI and Bauhaus Kooperation object pages

convergences.label: Founding of the Staatliches Bauhaus in Weimar
convergences.note: The official record is a change of name; Gropius's manifesto promises a guild of craftsmen; Feininger's woodcut makes the promise visible as a shattered, radiant cathedral.

convergences.label: Itten goes, Moholy-Nagy comes, and the Landtag attacks
convergences.note: The same month the school lost its most charismatic teacher, it faced a formal interpellation in the Landtag. Gropius's turn to industry answered both critics, from opposite directions.

convergences.label: Bauhaus Week and the 1923 exhibition
convergences.note: Gropius presents the new unity of art and technology; Schlemmer's stage and murals show the older, theatrical Bauhaus, and his manifesto is pulled for its politics; Stölzl's workshop supplies the carpets that sell.

convergences.label: The masters dissolve the Weimar Bauhaus
convergences.note: The state's notices and budget cuts are recorded by the councils; the masters' declaration pre-empts them; Ise Gropius's new diary follows the search for a city that would take the school.

convergences.label: Opening of the Dessau building
convergences.note: For Gropius it was the school's manifesto in glass; Felix Klee remembered a community festival; Stölzl's looms had moved in weeks before.

convergences.label: Gropius resigns; Meyer takes over
convergences.note: Gropius hands over to the man he had recruited; Ise's diary ends with sharp remarks on the newcomer; Meyer begins by redirecting the school towards the people's needs.

convergences.label: Meyer dismissed; Mies appointed
convergences.note: Meyer called it an expulsion for his politics; Kandinsky and Gropius saw it as saving the school; Mies was brought in to keep it out of politics. The record supports each account of motive only in part.

convergences.label: The police search in Steglitz
convergences.note: Two days before the raid Feininger, on the Baltic, wrote of peace and distance from the world; in Berlin the building where Mies was teaching was searched and sealed.

convergences.label: Self-dissolution of the Bauhaus
convergences.note: The faculty's protocol speaks only of money; the Gestapo's letter, dated a day later, names Kandinsky among those who would have had to go.

ties.note: Feininger was the first master Gropius appointed in 1919 and designed the image on Gropius's manifesto.
Gropius brought Itten to Weimar (they had met in Alma Mahler's Vienna circle) and then fought him in 1921–22 over commerce and Mazdaznan until Itten left.
They married in October 1923; her 1924–28 diary records his last years as director from inside the household.
Gropius hired Meyer to found the architecture department and proposed him as his successor in 1928, and in 1930 urged his removal.
Mies was appointed to replace Meyer in August 1930 and to purge the school of the politics Meyer had tolerated.
From 1926 they lived in the two halves of one master's house in Dessau, friends since the Blue Rider years in Munich.
Stölzl took Itten's preliminary course in 1919 and in 1924 he sent her to set up the Mazdaznan weaving mill at Herrliberg.
Albers trained in the weaving workshop that Stölzl ran; both shaped it into a school of industrial textile design.
After running the metal workshop, Brandt left the Bauhaus in 1929 to work in Gropius's Berlin architectural office.
Schlemmer's stage work fitted poorly with Meyer's social-functional programme, and he left for Breslau in 1929.
Kandinsky sat on the faculty that voted with Mies to dissolve the school on 20 July 1933.
The Dessau council's 1932 vote drove Mies to move the school to Berlin, where the Dessau prosecutor's request led to the April 1933 search.
Colleagues from 1921 to 1931 and neighbours in the Dessau master's houses; both kept teaching loads light to protect their painting.

threads_out.note: Itten ran a private art school in Vienna until 1919 and brought students from it to Weimar; Gropius met him through Alma Mahler, his first wife and Gustav Mahler's widow, who later visited the Dessau Bauhaus. Kandinsky's 1923 attempt to bring Arnold Schoenberg to Weimar ended in their bitter exchange over antisemitism.
The school was founded by veterans of the Western Front, Gropius among them, and Gunta Stölzl had served as a Red Cross nurse; the manifesto's call for a new start grew directly out of the war's end.

Kandinsky spent the revolutionary years in Moscow working for the Soviet arts administration before leaving for the Bauhaus at the end of 1921; Stölzl and colleagues visited the Moscow Vkhutemas in 1928.

Hannes Meyer went to Moscow in autumn 1930 with a group of former Bauhaus students; several of those who stayed, among them Béla Scheffler and Philipp Tolziner, were arrested in the purges of 1937–38.

The closure of 1933 scattered the Bauhaus: Gropius, Mies, Moholy-Nagy and the Alberses went to the United States, Klee to Bern, Kandinsky to Paris; Schlemmer's and others' works were shown in the 1937 'Degenerate Art' exhibition, and some Bauhaus members died in the camps.
